strengths: Addresses a fundamental, timely, and widely recognized bottleneck in mechanistic interpretability: the brittleness and dataset-sensitivity of discovered circuits.

Formulates a rigorous and elegant theoretical framework by connecting randomized deletion smoothing (RS-Del) with per-component abstention to achieve worst-case edit-distance stability certificates for circuit components (Theorem 3.1).

Provides extensive experimental validation across two modalities (vision and language), three architectures (ResNet-50/101, ViT-B/16, GPT-2 Small), and four discovery algorithms, showing consistent improvements in both compactness and sufficiency/accuracy.

Demonstrates strong empirical transfer to out-of-distribution datasets (ImageNet-A, OOD-CV, ImageNet-C, ImageNet-O, and distractor prompt sets) and high stability across random seeds (mean IoU > 0.97).

Includes thoughtful computational analysis and optimizations (Appendix D), illustrating how caching intermediate per-example scores reduces the overhead of n=1,000 Monte Carlo samples to just ~2.4x of a single baseline run.
weaknesses: The certified radius under the primary vision setup (|D|=50) is modest (r = 1 edit). While Appendix F.4 demonstrates that larger radii (r up to 59) are achievable with larger concept datasets (|D| >= 500), the practical guarantee remains tight on small datasets.

The efficient caching mechanism relies heavily on discovery algorithms whose component scores decompose cleanly across individual examples (e.g., top-K relevance, activation, EAP-IG). For iterative or interventional search procedures like ACDC, where graph components are pruned sequentially based on whole-dataset performance, running n=1,000 samples would be computationally prohibitive.

In the vision sufficiency evaluation, non-circuit channels are ablated via zero-ablation. As noted in the mechanistic interpretability literature, zero-ablation can introduce out-of-distribution internal activations; comparing against mean-ablation or resample-ablation would provide stronger confirmation of circuit sufficiency.

While the comparison to majority vote (>50% threshold) in Figure 16 isolates the effect of the confidence threshold, the paper could more directly benchmark against heuristic bagging/bootstrap aggregation with tuned inclusion percentiles to clarify the exact empirical edge provided by the formal hypothesis-testing procedure.

strengths: Principled problem formulation: The paper tackles a well-documented and pressing challenge in mechanistic interpretability—the brittleness and dataset-overfitting of discovered circuits—by introducing the first framework with formal stability guarantees against dataset-level edit perturbations.

Sound and elegant theoretical framework: Combining deletion-based randomized smoothing (RS-Del) with per-component abstention (SEGCERTIFY) translates structured output certification into the circuit discovery domain seamlessly. The guarantees hold with rigorous statistical confidence control (Clopper-Pearson and Bonferroni FWER).

Comprehensive empirical validation: Experiments span vision (ResNets, ViT-B/16 across ImageNet and four diverse OOD benchmarks) and language (GPT-2 Small on IOI, IOI-Hard, Greater-Than) across multiple attribution scorers (relevance, activation, rank, EAP-IG).

Favorable trade-off and practical gains: Instead of suffering from the classic robustness-accuracy trade-off, Certified Circuits simultaneously yield higher sufficiency (cACC) and significantly higher compactness (up to 80% fewer edges/neurons), filtering out spurious correlations as confirmed by qualitative patch visualizations.

Thorough ablations and computational analysis: The appendix provides extensive characterizations of sample complexity, certified radius vs. dataset size, comparison to vanilla majority voting, run-to-run seed stability (pairwise IoU > 0.95), and an efficient caching strategy reducing overhead to ~2.4x.
weaknesses: Incremental theoretical novelty: The theoretical machinery (Theorem 3.1) is largely a direct application of RS-Del (Huang et al., 2023) and segmentation smoothing with abstention (Fischer et al., 2021) to the circuit discovery setting, rather than introducing fundamentally new smoothing bounds.

Conservative radius in standard vision settings: In the main vision experiments where concept datasets have typical sample sizes (|Dc| = 50), the certified radius is limited to r = 1 edit. While Appendix F.4 demonstrates scaling up to r = 59 for larger |Dc|, real-world concept-based interpretability datasets are frequently small.

Evaluation on language is limited to smaller models and synthetic benchmarks: The language experiments evaluate GPT-2 Small on relatively standard, template-based mechanistic tasks (IOI, Greater-Than). Validating the approach on larger open-weights LLMs (e.g., Llama-3) or more open-ended reasoning tasks remains an open direction.

strengths: Principled and novel formulation: The paper bridges randomized smoothing (specifically RS-Del and per-component abstention) with mechanistic interpretability, providing the first dataset-level certified robustness guarantees for discovered circuits against bounded edit perturbations.

Sound theoretical framework: Theorem 3.1 rigorously bounds circuit component invariance under Levenshtein edit distance, accompanied by rigorous finite-sample hypothesis testing with Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) control via Bonferroni correction.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across two modalities (vision and language), multiple model families (ResNet-50/101, ViT-B/16, GPT-2 Small), and multiple discovery algorithms (relevance, activation, rank top-K, and EAP-IG), demonstrating consistent improvements in circuit compactness (up to 80% edge reduction) and sufficiency.

Practical computational feasibility: The caching optimization presented in Appendix D avoids the naive O(n) forward/backward scaling, reducing the overhead of drawing n=1,000 samples to approximately 2.4x the wall-clock cost of the uncertified baseline.

Extensive analysis and ablation studies: The paper thoroughly examines structural stability across distribution shifts (IoU analysis), stability across random seeds (mean IoU > 0.97), feature visualizations of abstained vs. retained units, and isolates the effect of the confidence threshold tau over simple majority voting.
weaknesses: Modest certified radius on standard vision benchmarks: For standard ImageNet concept sets (|D_c| = 50), the certified radius is r = 1, which guarantees invariance against only a single image addition, deletion, or replacement. While Appendix F.4 shows scaling to larger radii when larger sample sizes are available, the formal guarantee on standard small-sample setups is limited.

Potential specificity / false positive confounding in sufficiency evaluation: In vision, sufficiency (cACC) is evaluated by restricting the network to class circuit C_c and testing only on images from class c. Pruning channels not associated with class c naturally suppresses competing class logits, which helps explain dramatic jumps in accuracy (e.g., ImageNet-A accuracy jumping from 7% for the full model to 94% for the circuit). Evaluating specificity (e.g., false positive rate or behavior on non-concept inputs) alongside sufficiency would provide a more complete picture.

Theoretical reliance on existing smoothing primitives: The mathematical machinery is primarily a direct synthesis of RS-Del (Huang et al., 2023) and SegCertify (Fischer et al., 2021). While the conceptual application to dataset-to-circuit mapping is original, the underlying smoothing proofs are largely direct adaptations.

Model scale in NLP: Evaluation on language models is restricted to GPT-2 Small. Validating on larger, modern open-source LLMs (e.g., Llama or Gemma variants) would strengthen the empirical claims regarding scalability to state-of-the-art architectures.

strengths: The paper introduces an original and conceptually interesting framing by formalizing circuit discovery as a dataset-to-subnetwork mapping and applying deletion-based randomized smoothing (RS-Del) to provide worst-case stability certificates under dataset edits.
The framework is algorithm-agnostic and model-agnostic, treating the circuit discovery procedure as a black box and inducing adaptive sparsity by abstaining on unstable components.

The manuscript is clearly written and provides extensive empirical evaluations on ImageNet across four challenging out-of-distribution benchmarks (OOD-CV, ImageNet-A, ImageNet-O, ImageNet-C) using multiple neuron scoring functions (Relevance, Activation, Rank).
weaknesses: The practical certified radius is virtually vacuous: in Section 4, the authors select $p_{\text{del}} = 0.6$ and $\tau = 0.95$, which evaluates via Theorem 3.1 to a certified radius of $r = 1$. Under the stated condition $\text{dist}_{\text{edit}}(D, D') < r$, $r=1$ guarantees invariance only for an edit distance of 0 (no edits), or at best a single insertion/deletion/substitution on datasets containing hundreds of images. This creates a significant disconnect between the paper's motivational claims of provable robustness against practitioner edits and the actual theoretical guarantee achieved.

The empirical gains are not disentangled from classical stability selection / bagging: the procedure of running discovery on 1,000 sub-datasets and retaining components selected with high frequency is essentially stability selection (Meinshausen & Bühlmann, 2010). The paper does not provide an ablation comparing against simple heuristic subsample ensembling/thresholding to establish whether the certification machinery itself provides practical advantages beyond standard bagging.

The evaluation is restricted to channel-level pruning in CNNs (ResNet-50/101) with top-$K$ heuristics, omitting modern transformer-based circuit discovery methods (e.g., ACDC, EAP-IG, edge/head-level patching) where dataset instability is most frequently debated. Furthermore, requiring $n=1,000$ discovery runs poses severe computational hurdles for iterative discovery algorithms like ACDC.

The evaluation metric (cACC under sufficiency pruning) shows extreme disparities—such as the certified subnetwork achieving 94% on ImageNet-A where the full ResNet-101 achieves only 9%—that likely arise from severe logit suppression of competing classes rather than genuine OOD classification capability. The paper lacks adequate discussion and control for this class-logit calibration artifact.

strengths: Important problem: The paper tackles an established and pressing challenge in mechanistic interpretability—namely, that discovered circuits can be fragile and overfit to the specific dataset used for discovery.
Principled framing of stability: Formulating dataset-level stability guarantees via randomized smoothing (specifically RS-Del) and per-component abstention is a creative concept.

Comprehensive empirical benchmarks: The empirical evaluation explores ResNet-50 and ResNet-101 across standard in-distribution ImageNet and four diverse out-of-distribution shifts (OOD-CV, ImageNet-A, ImageNet-O, ImageNet-C), investigating sufficiency, compactness, and structural overlap (IoU).
weaknesses: Vacuous certified radius in practical evaluation: In Section 4, the parameters chosen are $p_{\text{del}} = 0.6$ and $\tau = 0.95$, which yield a certified radius of $r = 1$ (where $r = \lfloor \log(1.5 - \tau) / \log p_{\text{del}} \rfloor$). Under the condition $\text{dist}_{\text{edit}}(D, D') < 1$, this certificate guarantees invariance only for an edit distance of zero (i.e., no edits allowed) or at best a single edit. On datasets consisting of hundreds or thousands of images, guaranteeing stability against $\le 1$ sample addition/deletion is practically vacuous.

Critical evaluation confound in sufficiency pruning (cACC): The reported metric, mean circuit class accuracy (cACC), evaluates the pruned subnetwork $C_c$ exclusively on target-class images $D_c$. Pruning 60–70% of channels specific to other classes severely impairs the network's ability to output competing class logits. As a result, the argmax over 1,000 classes trivially defaults to class $c$, artificially inflating accuracy to 94–96% even on challenging benchmarks like ImageNet-A (where the full model achieves only 9%). The paper does not measure the false-positive rate for class $c$ on non-target images (i.e., whether $C_c$ simply predicts class $c$ for any input). The reported 'oACC' in Table 2 merely measures whether $C_c$ correctly predicts the true labels of other classes, which naturally drops to ~0% when non-target channels are ablated.

Limited novelty over existing smoothing frameworks: The theoretical result (Theorem 3.1) is a direct application of the RS-Del certificate (Huang et al., 2023) combined with coordinate-wise abstention thresholds (Fischer et al., 2021). The underlying smoothing procedure is essentially stability selection / bagging applied to channel pruning heuristics (top-K activation/attribution).

Scope of mechanistic circuits: The paper restricts 'circuits' to coarse-grained channel subsets in standard convolutional residual blocks, which aligns more closely with classical filter pruning / subnetwork identification than with edge-level, causal graph discovery in modern mechanistic interpretability (e.g., attention heads, MLP neurons, edge pruning via ACDC).

strengths: Important problem: Addressing the dataset sensitivity, brittleness, and lack of out-of-distribution stability in mechanistic interpretability is a timely and valuable research direction.
Interesting conceptual angle: Connecting randomized smoothing (specifically deletion-based smoothing) to interpretability and subnetwork extraction is an intriguing perspective.

Extensive experimental breadth: The authors evaluate multiple scoring metrics (activation, relevance, rank) across two architectures (ResNet-50 and ResNet-101) on standard in-distribution ImageNet as well as four distribution shift benchmarks (OOD-CV, ImageNet-A, ImageNet-O, and ImageNet-C).
weaknesses: Potential evaluation artifact and lack of false-positive testing (Soundness): The reported sufficiency gains (cACC) and 'specificity' results (oACC) exhibit strong signs of a trivial classification collapse. Specifically, evaluating a class-c subnetwork only on class-c inputs (Table 1) yields an implausible jump on ImageNet-A from 9% (full model) to 94% (certified circuit). When non-target channels are pruned, remaining channels disproportionately favor class c, which often leads to the pruned model predicting class c for almost any input. In Table 2, the authors define specificity via other-class accuracy (oACC, predicting the true label of non-target images) and celebrate that oACC drops to 0–1%. However, if a subnetwork trivially predicts class c on all inputs, its oACC on other classes is automatically 0%. To demonstrate true concept specificity, the authors must report the False Positive Rate (how frequently Cc predicts class c when given images from other classes).

Practically vacuous certified radius: In Section 4, the authors choose hyperparameters p_del = 0.6 and tau = 0.95, which yields a certified radius of r = 1. According to Theorem 3.1, the invariance guarantee holds for dist_edit(D, D') < r. Because edit distance is an integer, dist_edit(D, D') < 1 implies dist_edit = 0 (no edit at all). Even under a non-strict inequality (r <= 1), certifying invariance against a single insertion, deletion, or substitution in a dataset containing dozens or hundreds of images provides negligible theoretical protection against dataset perturbation.

Formulation mismatch (Sequence edit distance vs. unordered datasets): Datasets are unordered sets, yet the paper applies RS-Del, which is designed for ordered sequences under Levenshtein edit distance. The authors note that they fix an arbitrary ordering, but Levenshtein distance on sequences is sensitive to index positions. For example, simply reordering/permuting an identical set of images yields a massive edit distance up to |D|, even though the dataset itself is unchanged.

Disconnect from mechanistic interpretability and limited technical novelty: The algorithmic pipeline amounts to subsampling-based stability selection (bagging) applied to coarse channel pruning at the outputs of four ResNet residual blocks. The theoretical framework is a direct application of RS-Del (Huang et al., 2023) combined with per-component smoothing from Fischer et al. (2021), without tailoring the theory to computational subgraphs, edge attribution, or mechanistic circuits.
